title: Stravinsky, Beethoven and playing the past alive
summary: Music must live; the Juilliard Quartet's roaring Beethoven.

blocks.x: If I may be the evil's advocate for amooment, is not what you say of say an Ellington piece from 1940, being reflective of that period, isn't that as true say of (inaudible) reflecting Stravinsky's attitudes in the early twentieth century?
I think it is; I think it is very much so.
I think that two things have been raised here. One is the approach towards music that Stravinsky had, which was (inaudible). It is definitely that period that is nothing else but that.

I was listening last night to Julliard making a broadcast on WNTN and Channel 13; there was something about it that made we want to listen. One of the things the man said is that they tried, in that quartet, to make classical music seem modern, and modern music seem classical and there was a question on how that was and why they did that. He didn't like the arbitrary of using that aspect, say on Beethoven, where you sit at the master's seat with great reverence and play each phrase of each situation that has been passed down by rote through the years--
As if it were engraved in stone.

Yeah. And missing the real point of the thing possibly in the process, so that all you're doing is imitating--or you're following the rules set down by almost everyone else than Beethoven, something else of the period that Beethoven wrote it, the cultural feel of that period. Subsequent cultures don't really respond to that.

His music, as played by the Julliard quartet, and especially the (inaudible) quartet, it roared--Beethoven roared. Such a magnificent great man. (Inaudible). If you can bring a sense of enduring or substance to a contemporary piece (inaudible).
Assuming that that attitude is present, is it possible
I think what's important is to get the essence of what that was and to build on it and not to imitate it, to make it come alive. In other words, it has to live; if it doesn't live it's nothing.
